chapters.name: Chapter 1: Your voice and your prompts

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing your brand voice guide
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page guide that tells any AI tool how you sound.
This lesson builds toward: Using five of your own captions and an AI assistant, you will write a one-page brand voice guide, with three voice words, words you use and never use, topics to post and avoid, emoji and hashtag habits, and two sample posts.
AI writes in a generic voice unless you tell it how you sound. A brand voice guide fixes that, and also helps teammates or family who help with your posts.
Your guide has: three words for your voice (for example "confident, grateful, funny"); words and phrases you use; words you never use; topics you post about; topics you avoid; emoji and hashtag habits; and two sample posts that sound exactly like you.
Ask an AI assistant to help: paste five of your best captions and ask, "Describe the voice in these posts in three words, and list phrases I repeat." Then edit the result.
Step by step:
- Collect five captions that sound like you.
- Ask AI to describe your voice.
- Pick three voice words.
- List words you use and never use.
- Add topics to post and avoid, and two sample posts.
Words to know:
- Brand voice: the personality and style of how you write and speak.
- Style guide: a document of rules so content stays consistent.
Try it now: Paste five of your captions into an AI assistant and ask it to describe your voice. Write your one-page guide from the result.
You can now write a brand voice guide that keeps AI output sounding like you.

check.q: Why does AI need a voice guide?
options: It writes in a generic voice unless you tell it how you sound
It cannot write captions without one
check.why: A voice guide tells AI and helpers how you sound.

check.q: Your little brother helps post for you. How does your voice guide help?
options: It shows him how you sound and what you never post
check.why: The guide helps teammates or family who help with your posts.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a prompt library
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Save ten reusable prompts for your most common marketing jobs.
This lesson builds toward: Given your most common marketing jobs, you will create a library of ten reusable prompts with blanks, each one referring to your voice guide and saved in one document.
A prompt library is a document of prompts you reuse. Instead of starting from zero each time, you copy a prompt, fill in the blanks and paste in your voice guide.
Good prompts have blanks in brackets: "Using my voice guide below, write three captions under 150 characters for a [type] post about [topic]. End with a question." Others: bio options, sponsor pitch email, thank-you note, post ideas for a pillar, a polite reply to a negative comment, a weekly recap.
Keep the library in Google Docs or a notes app. Improve a prompt each time it gives you a weak answer.
Step by step:
- List your ten most common marketing jobs.
- Write a prompt for each with [blanks].
- Add "Using my voice guide below..." to each.
- Save them in one document.
- Improve a prompt whenever it gives a weak answer.
Words to know:
- Prompt library: a saved collection of prompts you reuse.
- Template prompt: a prompt with blanks you fill in each time.
Try it now: Write your first five template prompts with [blanks]. Test one with your voice guide and fix it if the answer is weak.
You can now build and use a prompt library for your marketing jobs.

options: A document of prompts you reuse
check.why: It is a saved set of prompts you copy, fill in and reuse.

check.q: You often reply to negative comments. What do you add to your library?
options: A list of people to block
A prompt for a polite reply with [blanks] and your voice guide
check.why: Save a prompt for each common job, including polite replies.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choosing one tool per job
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick one tool for writing, design, video and tracking.
This lesson builds toward: Given the jobs of writing, design, video and tracking, you will choose one tool for each job, with each new tool's maker, data use and cost after any trial checked.
You need four jobs covered. Writing: an AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini. Design: a tool like Canva, which has templates and AI features. Video: a free editor like CapCut or the editors built into Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. Tracking: each app's insights plus a Google Sheet.
Choose one per job and learn it well. Before signing up for anything new, check who makes it, what data it collects, and what it costs after any free trial.
Many apps also let you schedule posts in advance, either inside the app or with scheduling tools. Scheduling helps during busy weeks, but check scheduled posts still make sense if news or results change.
Step by step:
- Pick a writing tool.
- Pick a design tool.
- Pick a video editor.
- Set up a tracking sheet.
- Write the four choices in your toolkit document.
Words to know:
- Scheduling: setting a post to publish automatically at a later time.
- Insights: an app's numbers about how your posts perform.
Try it now: Write your four tool choices in your toolkit document and set up a tracking sheet with columns: Date, Post, Platform, Views, Engagement, Notes.
You can now choose a small set of tools that covers every marketing job.

check.q: Which tool fits the tracking job?
options: Each app's insights plus a Google Sheet
check.why: Tracking uses app insights and a spreadsheet.

check.q: Your game was cancelled and a scheduled post says "See you tonight!". What do you do?
options: Change or cancel the scheduled post
check.why: Check scheduled posts still make sense when news changes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The five-point review checklist
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Review AI-made content with a five-point checklist before posting.
This lesson builds toward: Given any AI-made post, you will check it with the five-point review: true, voice, rights, disclosure and safe, passing all five checks before it goes public.
AI saves time, but you are responsible for everything you post. Run every piece through five checks.
1. True: every fact, stat and claim is correct. 2. Voice: it sounds like you (read it out loud). 3. Rights: you own or may use every photo, logo, clip and song. 4. Disclosure: any brand payment or free product is clearly disclosed. 5. Safe: no private info, live location or anything you'd regret.
Put the checklist at the top of your toolkit document. When someone helps you post, they use it too.
Step by step:
- True: check facts and stats.
- Voice: read it out loud.
- Rights: check photos, logos, clips and music.
- Disclosure: brand ties clearly stated.
- Safe: no private info or live location.
Words to know:
- Review checklist: a short list of checks done before anything is published.
- Responsible: you answer for what is posted, even if AI wrote it.
Try it now: Take one AI-written caption and run the five checks. Write what you changed for each check.
You can now review AI content for truth, voice, rights, disclosure and safety.

options: Do you own or have permission for every photo, logo, clip and song?
check.why: Rights means you may use everything in the post.

check.q: An AI caption mentions the park where you train every morning at 6. Which check catches it?
check.why: The Safe check removes private info and live location or routine.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Rights, logos, music and disclosure
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify what you may use in your content and write a clear disclosure for brand ties.
This lesson builds toward: Given photos, logos, music and brand ties in your content, you will identify what you may use and write a clear disclosure for any brand connection, with permission for every item you did not make, licensed music, no misleading AI images and the disclosure in the post itself.
Rights: you can use photos and videos you made, and ones you have permission for. Team and game photos taken by others belong to the photographer or school, so ask. School, league and brand logos need permission. Use music from an app's licensed library.
AI images: be careful making AI pictures of real people, teammates, or brand logos. Do not make images that could fool people into thinking something happened that did not.
Disclosure: the FTC says to clearly disclose any payment, free product or other connection to a brand, in the post itself, using clear words like "Ad" or "Thanks [brand] for the free gear". Student-athletes: check NIL rules with your compliance office or state athletic association.
Step by step:
- Use your own photos or ones you have permission for.
- Ask before using logos.
- Use licensed music.
- Don't make misleading AI images of real people.
- Disclose brand ties clearly in each post.
Words to know:
- Copyright: the owner's legal right to control copies of photos, video, music and writing.
- Permission: a clear yes from the owner to use their work.
Official sources:
- FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
Try it now: Look at your last five posts. For each photo, clip and song, write who owns it and whether you had permission. Fix or remove anything that fails.
You can now use only content you have rights to and disclose brand ties correctly.

check.q: Who usually owns game photos taken by a school photographer?
options: You, because you are in them
check.why: Photos taken by others belong to the photographer or school, so ask.

check.q: You want an AI image of your teammate holding a trophy they never won. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to make it more real
Do not make it; it could fool people
check.why: Do not make AI images that could fool people into thinking something happened.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tracking results and improving the toolkit
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track results weekly and use them to improve your prompts and plan.
This lesson builds toward: After a week of posting, you will record your numbers in a tracking sheet and update your prompts and voice guide from the results, with top and bottom posts named and any AI reading checked against the sheet.
Once a week, copy your posts' numbers from each app's insights into your tracking sheet: views, engagement (likes, comments, shares, saves) and anything tied to your goal, like link clicks or sign-ups.
Find your top and bottom posts. Paste the table into an AI assistant and ask: "Which types of posts did best and what do they have in common? Give me two ideas for next week." Check its reading against the sheet.
Then improve your toolkit: update the prompt that made your best post, fix the one behind your worst, and add any new lesson to your voice guide.
Step by step:
- Copy weekly numbers into your sheet.
- Find top and bottom posts.
- Ask AI what the top posts share.
- Check its answer against the sheet.
- Update your prompts and voice guide.
Words to know:
- Engagement: how people interact: likes, comments, shares, saves.
- Iterate: improve something step by step based on results.
Try it now: Final task: finish your toolkit document (voice guide, ten prompts, four tools, five-point checklist), then make one post from start to finish with it and log its numbers in your sheet.
You can now track results and keep improving your AI marketing toolkit.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Brand voice guide Missing voice words, never-use words or sample posts. One page with three voice words, use and never-use words, topics, habits and two sample posts. Built from real captions and tested by having AI write a post that a friend says sounds like the learner. Prompt library Fewer than ten prompts, or prompts with no blanks or voice guide. Ten prompts with [blanks], each using the voice guide, saved in one document. At least one prompt has been improved after a weak answer, with a note on what changed. Tool choices A job is missing a tool, or tools were not checked. One tool each for writing, design, video and tracking, with maker, data and cost checked. Includes a note on when scheduling is used and how scheduled posts are checked. Review checklist Checklist missing or incomplete. The five checks are at the top of the toolkit document. Helpers who post for the learner have agreed to use it. One post start to finish The post fails a check, such as rights or disclosure. One post made with the toolkit that passes all five checks, with permitted media and any disclosure in the post. Its numbers are recorded in the tracking sheet and used to update a prompt. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How often should you copy your numbers into your tracking sheet?
Your best post came from one saved prompt. What do you do?
options: Update and keep improving that prompt
check.why: Update the prompt that made your best post and fix the one behind your worst.
